1.text:
How Did Earth Keep Its Air When Mars Lost So Much?

We've been inside the Earth and we've read its rocks. Now we're heading up into the air, and then out into space to the invisible magnetic bubble that surrounds our planet.

Here's the mystery. Mars once had thicker air and even liquid water, but today its air is thin and cold. Earth kept a thick, comfortable atmosphere. What made the difference? You might think it's Earth's magnetic field, and that's part of the story. But Venus has no magnetic field and still has a crushingly thick atmosphere, so the real answer is messier.

We'll go in four steps: what the air is made of and how life changed it, the layers of the atmosphere, how the air handles heat, and finally the magnetic shield.

Did you know? Saturn's moon Titan has a thicker atmosphere than Earth does, even though it's a moon.

2.text:
Today I Can...

Here's what you'll be able to do by the end of this deck. Copy these into your notebook as "I can" statements and rate yourself 1 to 3 on each one.

I can describe what air is made of and how outgassing and life changed it. I can model the composition, layers and circulation of gases. I can make a flowchart of how carbon and oxygen move between air, life, ocean and rock. I can read the temperature profile and explain air pressure and ozone. I can explain the greenhouse effect as a mechanism, plus albedo. I can model how land and water heat differently and drive breezes.

I can also explain how the fluid outer core makes the magnetosphere, and how the magnetosphere protects people and satellites. I can link magnetic reversals to the seafloor stripes from Deck 9. And, as an enrichment goal, I can compare the air and shields of Venus, Mars and Titan.

3.text:
What Is Air Made Of?

An atmosphere is the layer of gases that a planet's gravity holds around it. So what's in ours? On this chart, 1 dot = 1% of the air. Most of the dots are nitrogen, N2: 78%. Next comes oxygen, O2: 21%. Argon, Ar, is about 1%.

That leaves just a sprinkle for everything else. Carbon dioxide (CO2) was about 427 ppm in 2025 (the annual average, measured by NOAA). Ppm means "parts per million," so that's roughly 4 molecules out of every 10,000. Water vapor shows up only in traces and changes with the weather.

Don't let the small numbers fool you. CO2 and water vapor are trace gases, but they have a big effect on Earth's temperature, as you'll see on Slide 12.

Did you know? Air isn't weightless. It presses on every square centimeter of you with about 1.03 kg.

4.text:
Life Changed the Air

Earth's first air didn't look anything like today's. Gas came from outgassing (gas escaping from inside the planet through volcanoes) and from impacts of comets and asteroids. Those sources gave the early air CO2, H2O and N2, but no oxygen. Follow the timeline: when Earth formed, there was no O2 at all.

Then life got to work. Tiny cyanobacteria grew in mats and built rocky mounds called stromatolites. They made oxygen by photosynthesis. At first, rocks soaked up the oxygen as fast as it formed. But about 2.4 billion years ago, O2 finally built up in the air: the Great Oxidation Event, or GOE.

With oxygen in the air, the ozone layer could form, and that made life on land possible. Today the air is 21% O2. Living things rebuilt the atmosphere.

Did you know? You may see "about 2 billion years ago" in some books. The oxygen rise took a long time, roughly 2.4 to 2.3 billion years ago, so sources round it differently.

5.text:
Model It: Air & Its Cycles

Time to build two models. For Model A, draw the atmosphere. Use the gas percentages from Slide 3, the five layers with their heights (you'll learn them on Slide 7), and show warm air rising and cool air sinking.

For Model B, make a carbon and oxygen flowchart. Show where O2 and CO2 enter and leave the atmosphere, biosphere (living things), ocean and rock. Include photosynthesis and respiration, plus volcanoes, oceans and burning fuels. Add methane (CH4) from farming, livestock and rice paddies. And don't forget the oceans: warmer oceans hold less CO2, so they release more, like a soda going flat on a hot day.

Mark each arrow: does that process speed up or slow down the cycle? Draw both models, and label every arrow with the process that moves the gas.

Did you know? Most of Earth's carbon isn't in the air at all. It's locked in rocks and dissolved in the ocean.

6.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 1

Think back to the timeline on Slide 4. Where did most of the O2 in our air come from?

Is it A) volcanic outgassing, B) photosynthesis by microbes and plants, C) comets that hit Earth, or D) the solar wind? Choose your answer and explain why the other three can't be the main source.

7.text:
The Air Is Layered by Temperature

If you rode an elevator straight up into space, the temperature wouldn't just keep dropping. It zigzags! Scientists use those temperature changes to divide the air into layers.

The troposphere is the lowest layer, where almost all weather happens. It reaches 6 to 20 km up (taller at the equator, shorter at the poles), and the temperature falls from about 17 °C to about -51 °C at the top. Next is the stratosphere, up to 50 km. Here the temperature rises to about -15 °C, because ozone warms it. Then the mesosphere, up to 85 km, gets colder again, down to about -90 °C at its top, sometimes colder. It's where meteors burn up.

Above 85 km, the thermosphere heats up to 2,000 °C higher up. But there are so few molecules that it would actually feel cold to you. Beyond that, the exosphere starts above 600 km and fades into space. Many satellites orbit up in the thermosphere and exosphere. The ISS orbits in the thermosphere, about 400 km up.

Did you know? Warm air sitting over cold air in the stratosphere acts like a lid, which is why big thunderstorms flatten out into anvil shapes at the top.

8.text:
Air Has Weight

All the air above you has weight, and it presses down on you all the time. Standard pressure at sea level is 1013 mb (millibars). That's the same as 29.92 inches of mercury on a weather report, or about 1.03 kg pressing on each cm2.

Why don't you feel squished? Because the pressure pushes in all directions, including from inside your body, so it balances out.

Pressure falls as you go up, because there's less air stacked above you. The air gets thinner up high, and denser near the ground. In fact, half of all air is below 5.6 km. By 30 km, the air is very thin.

Did you know? Weather maps adjust every station's reading to sea level, so places at different heights can be compared fairly.

9.text:
The Ozone Layer Is Our Sunscreen

The ozone layer is stratospheric O3 that absorbs most of the Sun's UV light. O3 means 3 oxygen atoms stuck together. O2, the oxygen we breathe, has just 2. About 90% of all ozone sits in this layer, 10 to 50 km up.

Ozone works like sunscreen, but it blocks some kinds of UV better than others. UV-C, the most dangerous kind, is all blocked. UV-B is mostly blocked. UV-A gets through, because ozone absorbs little of it. Too much UV causes sunburn and can lead to skin cancer and eye damage.

Absorbing UV releases heat, which is why the stratosphere gets warmer as you go up. And here's a link to Slide 4: oxygen from life made the ozone layer possible, and the ozone layer made it safe for life to move onto land.

Did you know? The "ozone hole" isn't a hole in the whole atmosphere. It's a thinning of ozone over Antarctica, caused largely by human-made chemicals called CFCs.

10.text:
Titan's Air Is Thicker Than Ours

Saturn's moon Titan is the only moon with a thick atmosphere. Its surface pressure, measured by the Huygens probe, is 1.47 bar, about 45% more than Earth's. Earth's is about 1 bar.

Titan's air is a lot like ours in one way: it's mostly nitrogen. Titan's is 95% N2 and 5% methane (CH4), while Earth's is 78% N2. But Titan's gravity is weaker, so its atmosphere puffs way out. Its haze reaches 600 km up, while Earth's air is a thin shell by comparison.

Here's a key detail for later. Titan has no magnetic field of its own: it orbits inside Saturn's. So a world can hold a thick atmosphere without its own field.

Did you know? NASA's Titan page says the pressure is about 60% greater than Earth's. The Huygens measurement gives 45%, which is the number this course uses.

11.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 2

Look back at the zigzag temperature line on Slide 7. Why does the stratosphere get warmer as you go up?

Is it A) it is closer to the Sun, B) ozone absorbs UV and releases heat, C) hot air rises from the ground, or D) clouds trap heat there? Pick an answer and explain it. Hint: think about how far away the Sun really is compared to 50 km.

12.text:
The Greenhouse Effect

You've probably heard the greenhouse effect described as a "blanket." Let's see how it actually works, step by step. First, sunlight passes through the air. Nitrogen and oxygen let it right through, and it warms the ground. Second, the warm ground glows in infrared, an invisible kind of light we feel as heat.

Third, N2 and O2 let infrared pass, too. But CO2, H2O and CH4 absorb it. Fourth, those gas molecules re-emit the infrared up and down, in every direction. The part heading down is called back radiation, and it warms the ground even more. The surface keeps warming until it gives off as much energy as it takes in.

The result is a comfortable planet. Thanks to the natural greenhouse effect, Earth averages about 15 °C. Without it, Earth would be about 33 °C colder. The concern today is that burning fossil fuels adds more greenhouse gases and makes the effect stronger.

Did you know? Greenhouse gases don't block sunlight. They let most visible sunlight in and grab the infrared on its way out.

13.text:
Albedo: Bright Surfaces Bounce Sunlight

Albedo is how reflective a surface is. Earth reflects 29% of incoming sunlight right back to space. That reflected light never heats the planet at all.

What does the reflecting? Clouds reflect the most. Sea ice and snow are bright, and so is desert sand. Now look at the question marks: a city, a forest, and open water. How reflective are they?

You'll test the question-mark surfaces yourself in the heat lab on Slide 16. Predict now: which do you think reflects the least?

14.text:
Land & Water Heat Differently

Ever noticed that at the beach, the sand burns your feet while the water still feels cool? Land and water heat differently. Sunlight reaches deep into water, and waves keep mixing it, so water warms up slowly. On land, the Sun heats only the top few inches of soil, so land warms and cools fast.

That difference makes wind. A sea breeze is a daytime wind from cooler water toward warmer land. Here's how it works. Over the warm land, warm air rises, making a thermal low. Over the water, cool, dense air sinks and slides inland underneath. The leading edge is a sea breeze front. Up high, there's a return flow aloft, 1 to 1.5 km up, back out over the water.

It doesn't take an ocean. Lake Michigan makes these breezes too, next to warm land on a summer day.

Did you know? In winter, cold air crossing the warmer waters of Lake Michigan picks up moisture and dumps lake-effect snow downwind, which is why northern Indiana can get buried.

15.text:
Venus: A Runaway Greenhouse

Venus's average surface is 464 °C, under 92 bar of pressure. That's hotter than Mercury, even though Venus is farther from the Sun. The reason is a greenhouse effect that ran away.

A runaway greenhouse is a loop. More heat makes oceans evaporate. That puts more CO2 and H2O vapor into the air. More greenhouse gas traps even more heat, which evaporates even more water, and around and around it goes. If Venus did have oceans, once they were gone it could never get them back. (Some scientists think it may always have been dry.)

Compare the three neighbors. Venus: 96.5% CO2, 92 bar, 464 °C. Earth: 0.04% CO2, 1 bar, 15 °C. Mars: 95% CO2, but only 0.006 bar, so it's about -65 °C. Mars went the opposite way from Venus. Its air is mostly CO2, but it's so thin that it can't keep the planet warm.

Did you know? Earth has its own safety valve. Most of our CO2 is locked in rocks and dissolved in the oceans, not floating in the air.

16.text:
Heat Lab: What Warms Fastest?

Time to test the ideas from Slides 13 and 14 yourself. You'll set five surfaces under the same lamp: dry soil, light sand, water, white paper (standing in for ice), and black paper (standing in for a road).

For each surface, note whether it's light or dark, and record its temperature at the start, at 5 minutes, at 10 minutes, and at 15 minutes. Then work out the change in °C.

Then model it: draw heat in, heat reflected, and the breeze each pair would make. Finally, use your data to predict whether a city full of dark roofs and roads would be warmer or cooler than the fields around it. Make your prediction from your own numbers, and compare with other groups before you decide.

17.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 3

Use what you learned on Slide 12. Without any greenhouse gases, Earth's average surface would be...

A) about the same, 15 °C, B) well below freezing, C) hotter, near 464 °C, or D) boiling at the equator? Choose one and explain what greenhouse gases do for Earth's temperature.

18.text:
Earth's Core Is a Generator

Now for the shield. Deep inside Earth, the outer core is liquid iron, and the inner core is solid. That flowing liquid iron makes Earth's magnetic field, a process called the geodynamo.

It works as a loop. Convection moves the iron. Moving iron makes electric currents. Currents make the magnetic field. And the field keeps the loop going, as long as heat keeps the iron churning.

The field lines loop out of the planet and back in, a bit like the field of a bar magnet. But the magnetic axis isn't lined up perfectly with the spin axis. It's tilted about 10° off.

Did you know? Earth doesn't have a giant bar magnet inside. The core is far too hot for a permanent magnet. The field is made by moving liquid iron.

19.text:
The Field Flips

Remember the striped seafloor from Deck 9, Slide 11? Now you can see what made those stripes. Earth's magnetic field flips: north and south swap places. When it's normal, a compass points north like today. When it's reversed, the compass would point south.

At the ridge, new rock records whichever way the field points as it cools. Then it spreads away, getting older on both sides. That's why the stripes of normal and reversed rock match like mirror images.

It's been about 773,000 years since the last magnetic reversal. Reversals don't happen on a schedule. They're random, sometimes every 10,000 years or so, sometimes not for almost 40 million years.

Did you know? During a flip, the field weakens a lot, but it doesn't vanish. Earth still has a weaker, messier field with several poles.

20.text:
A Magnetic Bubble Around Earth

The magnetosphere is the region of space where Earth's magnetic field dominates. It's an invisible bubble around our planet. Streaming at it is the solar wind, about 400 km/s of charged particles flowing out from the Sun.

The solar wind squashes the bubble on the side facing the Sun. That front edge, the magnetopause, sits about 10 Earth radii away. On the night side, the wind stretches the field into a long tail, hundreds of Earth radii long. That's way past the Moon's orbit, at 60 Earth radii away. Picture water flowing around a rock in a stream.

The magnetosphere steers most solar wind particles around Earth. It traps some in the radiation belts, which can cause trouble for satellites. It protects people and the technology we depend on. It isn't a perfect force field, though. Some energy and particles leak in.

Did you know? In 1951, Ludwig Biermann figured out from comet tails that a wind must blow out from the Sun. Eugene Parker explained it in 1958, and spacecraft (Luna 1 in 1959, Mariner 2 in 1962) measured it.

21.text:
Auroras Trace the Field

An aurora is light given off when electrons guided by Earth's field hit oxygen and nitrogen. The electrons follow field lines down toward the poles. When they slam into gas atoms in the upper air, the atoms glow, a bit like a neon sign.

The glow forms a ring around each magnetic pole called the auroral oval. There's a south oval too, which makes the southern lights. Auroras are best seen at 60° to 75° latitude, in places like Alaska and northern Canada. They form curtains of rays, 80 to 500 km up.

During big solar storms, the ovals spread toward the equator, and auroras can be seen across most of the United States, Indiana included.

Did you know? Auroras aren't sunlight bouncing off polar ice. The light comes from Earth's own oxygen and nitrogen.

22.text:
Mars Lost Its Shield & Most of Its Air

Mars's surface pressure is only 0.6% of Earth's. Standing there, you'd need a pressure suit. So what happened?

Mars once had a global magnetic field, but its core stopped making one more than 3.5 billion years ago. Today only patches of crustal magnetism are left in its rocks. With no global shield, the solar wind reaches right into the upper air. NASA's MAVEN spacecraft watched gas being stripped away. About 75% of the escaping ions leave down the tail, and about 25% leave in a polar plume.

Mars is losing about 100 g of gas every second today, and roughly 10 to 20 times more during solar storms. Over billions of years, that adds up. MAVEN found that about two-thirds of its argon has already been lost to space. That loss helped turn a warmer, wetter Mars into the cold desert we see now.

Did you know? Mars's gravity is weak too. Gas escapes Mars at 5.03 km/s, less than half the speed needed to escape Earth.

23.text:
Is a Magnetic Shield Enough?

So Mars lost its field and its air. Case closed? Not quite. Venus has no global magnetic field either, yet it keeps a thick 92 bar atmosphere. Instead, the solar wind piles up its field around Venus. That's an induced magnetosphere: a weak shield made when the solar wind's field piles up around a planet.

Compare the three planets. Earth: global field yes, 1 bar, escape speed 11.2 km/s. Venus: global field no, 92 bar, escape speed 10.4 km/s. Mars: global field no, 0.006 bar, escape speed 5.0 km/s.

Here's the catch. One 2018 model study (Gunell and others) estimated that all three lose roughly 0.5 to 2 kg/s of gas in total today, counting every escape process, not just the ions MAVEN measured. It suggests a field may not prevent loss. Gravity, how active the young Sun was, and how much gas a planet started with all matter too. Scientists are still debating this one. The magnetic field clearly protects people and satellites, but whether it's what saves a planet's air is an open question.

24.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 4

Time to pull the magnetic shield story together. What makes Earth's magnetic field, and what does it protect?

Is it A) a solid magnet core; it shields us from the solar wind, B) the ozone layer; it shields us from UV light, C) flowing liquid iron; it shields people and satellites from solar wind, or D) flowing liquid iron; it alone keeps all our air? Look back at Slides 18, 20 and 23. Read every word of each choice carefully before you pick.

25.text:
Exit Ticket

You went from the air you breathe to the edge of space today. Show what you've learned with three questions.

First, where did the O2 you breathe come from, and when did it build up? Second, explain the greenhouse effect without using the word "blanket." Third, how does the outer core protect satellites, and why might Mars have lost its air?

When you're done, look back at your "I can" list from Slide 2 and rate yourself again.

26.text:
The Standards Behind This Lesson

This lesson follows the Indiana Earth and Space Science standards. Here's what they ask you to do, in plain words.

ES.4.1: model what's in Earth's atmosphere, where it is and how it moves, and show how carbon and oxygen trade places with living things, oceans, rock and industry. ES.4.2: model how heat moves, is kept and is reflected by air, land and water, including how cities, terrain, clouds, sea ice and open water change albedo. Look at local and global heat exchange, like sea and land breezes, lake effects, city heat islands and deep ocean currents.

ES.3.1: make flowcharts of how carbon and oxygen move between rock, water, life and air, including CO2 and methane, and explain how farming, industry, ocean temperature and volcanoes can speed up or slow down that cycling. ES.6.2: explain how Earth's liquid outer core makes the magnetosphere and how it protects people and satellites from the solar wind. And as a review of ES.6.4, you connected magnetic flips back to the plate tectonics timeline from Deck 9.
